Subtraction Game

Game StrategyLogicAlgorithms
Game: Take turns subtracting a lower number from one of the numbers above the line. The player with no move left loses.
How to play: Click a number above the line, then click a number below it to subtract. Tick Define to change those lower numbers.
How many numbers 20 Subtrahends 3 Max 20
Look for the math

Here is a whole board of little subtraction games at once. The surprising part is that each number has a hidden value, and adding those values with XOR tells the computer exactly what to do.

One heap, then many

With just one number and the subtractions 1, 2, …, s, the losing numbers are the multiples of s + 1: whatever you subtract, your opponent can bring it back to a multiple. So the heap's value is its remainder n mod (s+1). The cut-the-knot page says this makes the game the same as Scoring; the logic test checks that formula for every s from 1 to 8 and every heap size up to 100, and it holds exactly.

Grundy values and the XOR

For an arbitrary set of subtractions, a number's value is the smallest non-negative number not among the values it can move to — its Grundy number. A board is losing when the Nim-sum (the XOR) of all its values is zero. From a non-zero sum there is always a subtraction that makes it zero, and the computer looks for exactly that move; from zero it has to move at random. This is the same idea that solves Nim.

What the check found

The logic test recomputes every Grundy value with an independent recursion and compares it with the table the port uses. It checks the Scoring claim above, confirms that a restoring move exists from every non-zero board it tries, and compares a second transcription of the applet's computer with this one on 3,000 random boards across the whole option range. One quirk stays on the applet's side: it prints "Illegal Move" for subtracting more than a number, but still goes ahead and makes the number negative. This port follows the page's rule that only non-negative results are legal.

Try the default board with Define unchecked. Does the computer ever let you leave it with a zero Nim-sum?
